title: iPhone Duo: 6 highs and lows that defined my first 12 hours
content:
Macworld





By now you’ve seen the keynote, watched the ads, and read the early reviews. You know what the iPhone Duo’s features are. But what is it like to use it, right here at the launch?
We’re working on our iPhone Duo review, but as the Apple Stores open up today to hand over a precious few preorders and disappoint legions of would-be drop-in buyers, I wanted to share some initial impressions. Here are six things I discovered on my first day with the iPhone Duo.




Outside bad, inside great
When you have the fold folded, it’s not a great experience. Even with the home row and controls on the side, it’s the smallest iPhone display in many years, and most apps just aren’t formatted for the odd shape. Unless you’ve been clinging to your iPhone 13 mini all this time, you’re likely to find that even optimized apps, which put their controls off on the right edge to allow more vertical room, are frustratingly small.
If you are an iPhone mini diehard, the screen won’t bother you, but the massively fat and chunky form factor will. What good is a small screen when the phone is so thick and wide that it’s definitely not going to fit in the pocket of a pair of tight jeans?
The actual display quality is fine, and so is the outside selfie camera. But that outside screen is for quick-hit info checking, firing off a short reply, dialing a phone number, or asking Siri stuff. That said, there is one huge benefit: the keyboard. While it takes up like half the vertical space, the extra-wide shape makes the whole keyboard a lot larger and easier to use. It’s even wider than an iPhone 18 Pro Max keyboard, and the extra few millimeters really help.
However, the inside display is a delight and makes me want this same nanotexture treatment on all iPhones. It has a lovely paper-like feel to the touch and seriously cuts down on glare, while still remaining bright and sharp. Granted, blacks aren’t as deep as on a glossy screen, but it’s still very good, and the trade-off is totally worth it for all the glare (and crease) you don’t have to deal with.
When using the inner display, the Duo feels super thin and light, comfortable and easy to use. The more time you spend with the Duo unfolded, the more you love it.
A status bar and Dynamic Island upgrade
Without a camera cutout in the middle of the display (inside or out), Apple moved the Dynamic Island to the upper right corner. It surrounds the front camera when closed, and just pops up out of nowhere on the inner display.
It’s actually in a really great spot, expanding down vertically as necessary. I prefer it to the centered one, and it makes me want Apple to stuff the camera up in the corner on all future iPhones.
There’s a new status bar element beneath it that, again, is a step up from current iPhones. A bar at the top shows battery (with percentage if you like), the Wi-Fi symbol in the middle is your Wi-Fi strength, and a series of four dots underneath is your cellular strength. It’s a brilliant little mash-up that again, should make its way to other iPhones.

				
					

				
			The new status icon and Dynamic Island placement work great and make it easier to open Control Center.
Foundry




No information is lost, space is saved, and it takes all of two seconds to get used to the change. Plus, you can tap on it to show the entire Control Center (so you don’t have to do an awkward edge swipe), which is already my favorite thing. When you do, the symbols separate and expand to show more detail.
StandBy any time
Another trick the Duo can do that other iPhones can’t is enter Standby mode when not connected to power. Just lock the screen and then stick it in “tent” posture, and it becomes a nice little smart clock for your desk. Or open it partially like a book, and you get a two-page Standby mode view.
It’s clever, it’s fun, and it makes the “put my iPhone down on the desk while working” thing actually useful. I can see this being the preferred way for Duo owners to place their phone when out with friends—keeping their phone out of their hands while still letting them see the clock or showing a conversation-starting photo album.
Dear Apple, please give every iPhone with an always-on display the option to go into Standby mode when not connected to power. Even lying flat on a desk, it would be nice.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The cameras are (mostly) fine
The 48MP main camera is not as good as that on the iPhone 18 Pro, even if you ignore the aperture blades. It starts to get a little noticeable in low light. But it’s close, and it’s certainly good enough. The ultra-wide is as good as Apple’s best, and as useful as ever for macro shots.
Weirdly, you get like half the Pro camera controls from the iPhone 18 Pro. There’s no aperture control (of course), no histogram, no shutter speed. But you do get white balance, manual focus with focus peaking, and the new photographic styles with adjustable skin texture and grain.
The front-facing selfie camera has the center stage functions (auto-rotate and auto-zoom) introduced in the iPhone 17 line with the new 18-megapixel sensor, but this isn’t that sensor. It’s the older 12MP sensor, and the dynamic range and clarity just aren’t as good. It’s fine, but the newer 18MP sensor on the other recent iPhones is better.
But that inside selfie camera. Oh. Oh no. No, that’s a potato. It takes blurry, awful 4MP photos that have a bunch of post-processing to over-sharpen and restore some detail. It’s kind of good enough for a FaceTime call in good lighting, but it’s absolute trash compared to the selfie cam since iPhone X. If this is the cost of an under-display camera, I don’t want it.

				
					

				
			Zoom in and see how blurry and messy that inside selfie camera is.
Foundry




Here’s a neat trick, though: When you’re in selfie mode, you can flip the whole Duo around, and there’s a “Slide to show camera” bar that flips the interface to the outside screen while turning off the inside screen so you don’t accidentally interact with it. Then you can take a selfie with the 48MP main camera. It’s pretty awesome, really.
The apps matter most
There are three classes of iPhone Duo apps, and you’ll discover all of them while learning how crucial they are in the first five minutes of using your iPhone Duo.
Old garbage apps: These are apps that haven’t been updated for the dynamic sizing of iOS 27. They have a black bar on the side of the outside screen and appear centered against a black background on the inside screen (though you can swipe to move it from the center to either side). These apps suck on the Duo. They put their interface buttons on the bottom, which makes them feel even smaller, and they waste all that space.
A lot of old apps, small apps from small companies (like a local bank chain), and apps with notoriously bad UI design, such as most car apps or insurance apps. It’s just a terrible experience, and there are a lot of these that probably won’t ever be updated. Thankfully, you can force these apps into split view with a Duo-optimized app that’ll make the awful experience slightly better.

				
					

				
			The Ring app, and many others, look and feel really bad on the Duo.
Foundry




iOS 27 apps: Apps that updated to use iOS 27’s resizable and reconfigurable layout fare a lot better. When you use them on the inside screen, they fill the width and often give you a sidebar, or split info between an index and content. The Tesla app just updated to use this, as does Microsoft Outlook and Robinhood, among others. It’s something of a stopgap, but is a signal that the developer is working on a proper Duo app. In fact, Robinhood says a Duo-optimized app will be available on launch day.

				
					

				
			Apps optimized for iOS 27, like Outlook, work well on Duo, even if they don’t support the poses and special features.
Foundry




You still get interface elements that don’t use the left/right sidebars, and they don’t understand all the “poses” for Duo, but at least you can go from iPhone app outside to iPad app inside, essentially, and it’s really nice.
Duo-optimized apps: Oh, these are fun. When an app uses the Duo-specific developer frameworks, it will put the interface elements out of the way on the side, mitigating the tiny outside screen (somewhat). Inside, it will fill the display, morph to make correct use of portrait and landscape view, and many times, move stuff away from the crease when you slightly fold the Duo into “book” form.
This is how the Duo is meant to be used, and it’s really great when it’s there. Most of Apple’s apps work like this, as you would expect, but some don’t (I’m looking at you, Wallet and Apple Store). Third-party apps that have updated to Duo-optimized apps all feel great. MLB, Spotify, Slack, Yelp, Instagram, TikTok, Things, Fantastical, Carrot Weather…there are plenty of popular apps with full Duo support, and the experience when you use them is awesome.

				
					

				
			Apps that fully support Duo offer expansive views, more info, and morph to adjust to how you’re holding it.
Foundry




But just as many important apps don’t work well on Duo at all. Given the book-sized open position and glare-free, paper-like coating on the display, you would think ebook readers would prioritize Duo support. But Kindle is flat-out busted, and glitches out when you try to show the menu in reader mode. (I actually had to close the Duo and return the app to the outside screen just to get out of the page view!) The Libby app is in desperate need of an update, too.

				
					

				
			The Kindle app is flat-out broken on the Duo, and flips out when you try to show the menu.
Foundry




The app situation is currently all over the place. Gmail supports the iOS 27 reactive sizing, but has a poor layout for widescreen. Google News is an old-style iPhone app that looks and feels terrible on the big screen. Video apps like Netflix, Paramount+, and Prime Video have nice Duo optimizations, but Hulu and Disney+ do not. Lyft, yes. Uber, no. 
It’s the Wild West right now, and the situation changes daily. The number of apps you use that are Duo-optimized (or at least iOS 27 optimized) is a crucial part of how much you’ll like using this phone, and it’s a quickly moving target.
I miss Face ID already
You’ve seen a lot of early reviewers complain about the lack of Face ID. They are correct.
We get emails all the time from people who miss Touch ID and want it back. I guess they forget what it was like to unlock their iPhone with gloves, or wet/dirty hands, or to have to reach to a certain spot, or to have their lock screen notifications jump away because you accidentally opened your phone when you unlocked it.
All those experiences come right back with the iPhone Duo. Except one—Apple added a delay on the lock screen. When you put your finger on the side button at the lock screen, your phone unlocks so you can see your notifications, but it doesn’t open yet. A little message shows a fingerprint icon and “Rest to Open” at the top of the display, and your iPhone opens to the home screen after a short pause with your finger on the button.

				
					

				
			Apple should add an option to use the lock screen pause for Touch ID or not.
Foundry




In the first hour with the Duo alone, there were dozens of situations in which I wanted to fill in a password, download an app, or make a purchase that required me to authenticate with Touch ID. And every single time, I was reminded that I now had to do something where Face ID would simply automatically authenticate. I registered both thumbs and my index finger with Touch ID, and that certainly helps, but it’s still slower and more awkward than Face ID.
Touch ID is more annoying on the iPhone Duo than it was on old iPhones or on an iPad, because those devices are usually held just one way, so the sensor is always in the same place. You get a muscle memory for it. The Duo is held both ways: in one hand and in two. Portrait and landscape. Folded like a tent, folded like a book, unfolded, closed… It’s a strength that there are so many ways to use it, until you need to touch the damn side button for Touch ID.
Stay tuned for Macworld’s full review of the iPhone Duo as I continue my testing.
creator: Macworld

title: iPhone Duo guide: Release date, price, specs and first reviews
content:
Macworld





Apple’s first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, officially goes on sale today, Friday, October 23, but getting hold of one could prove difficult. Preorders opened on October 16 and delivery estimates slipped rapidly, with Macworld’s U.S. tracking showing waits stretching to January 25, 2027 within around half an hour. Apple is still accepting orders, but there is another option for buyers who don’t want to wait: Apple has confirmed that limited numbers of the iPhone Duo will be available for walk-in customers at Apple Stores in the U.S., U.K. and other selected markets on launch day. Supplies are expected to be extremely limited, however, and there’s no guarantee of getting one without a preorder. Prices start at $1,999/£1,999.
The Duo opens like a book from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a much larger 7.6-inch device. Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro.
The biggest difference is obviously the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo ships with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. Apple Pencil USB-C support is also coming later in 2026.
The other major changes are the 7.6-inch nano-texture inner display, Touch ID replacing Face ID, an A20 Pro processor with vapor-chamber cooling, and a dual-battery system designed around the two halves of the phone. Apple has also introduced camera features that exploit the second screen, including Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime.
Much of the pre-launch reporting proved accurate: the Duo name, book-style design, roughly 7.7- and 5.4-inch screens, Touch ID, two 48MP rear cameras, two front-facing cameras, A20 Pro, C2 modem, MagSafe and the white/dark-blue colors were all anticipated.
iPhone Duo at a glance
Apple’s first folding iPhone, with 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner displays.
Touch ID replaces Face ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button.
A20 Pro with vapor-chamber cooling, including a new 2nm manufacturing process.
Dual-battery architecture, giving up to 44 hours of video playback on the outer display.
Fold-specific iOS and camera features, including Split View, Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and hands-free use.
iPhone Duo: Top 10 features


Foldable designBook-style titanium design with precision hinge
Inner display7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
Outer display5.4-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
ProcessorA20 Pro, 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU
Neural EngineDual 16-core Neural Engine
AuthenticationTouch ID in side button
Rear cameras48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide
BatteryDual batteries; up to 44 hours video on outer screen
ConnectivityC2 modem, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, second-gen UWB
Storage256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB

 






iPhone Duo release date: When did it launch?
Apple announced the iPhone Duo on September 9, 2026, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Sales began on October 23, following preorders on October 16.
The October 23 launch covers more than 70 countries and regions, including the U.S. and U.K., with another 28 markets following on October 30. The Duo will also be available through Apple Stores, selected carriers and authorized retailers, although availability varies by market.
Buy iPhone Duo at Apple U.S. 
Buy iPhone Duo at Apple U.K. 


						

							


Has the iPhone Duo sold out? 
Initial delivery allocations sold out rapidly, but Apple has confirmed Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo stock for walk-in customers on October 23. 
As of October 23, Apple was quoting January 22, 2027 for delivery of the 256GB iPhone Duo in the U.S. and January 25, 2027 in the U.K. Estimates can change and depend on the configuration and delivery location.
Apple confirmed that its stores will have limited iPhone Duo stock for walk-in customers when sales begin on October 23. That offers another possibility for buyers facing long online delivery waits, but availability is not guaranteed and will vary by store.
If Apple’s delivery estimate is too far away, iPhone stock-checking services may help you locate another option. Apple Inventory Check monitors Apple Store availability, while TrackaLacker covers selected online retailers, including Best Buy and Walmart. Some notification features require registration or payment. 
Apple described preorder demand as “nothing short of extraordinary” and said it was working to get devices to customers as quickly as possible.
Supply constraints may also contribute to the backlog. A late-September report claimed that Apple and its manufacturing partners were experiencing low production yields. Long delivery waits therefore reflect the balance between demand and available supply, rather than revealing how many phones Apple has sold.


						

							


iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			
The iPhone Duo opens up like a book.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.
The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable. The inner display also has a replaceable top cover layer. AppleCare+ lists replacement at $19, although it must be replaced by Apple rather than peeled off like a conventional screen protector. Apple has not yet published the price without AppleCare+.
The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

				
					

				
			
The hinge from the outside.

Apple




There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.
Action button and Camera Control
There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.
However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.
Accessories
Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable: 
The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129
Both became available to order on October 16. And there are plenty more of the best cases for iPhone Duo in our test reviews.


						

							


Face ID, Touch ID and the notch
Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.
Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.
The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.
The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.
Future Duo models could restore Face ID. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple has tested iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with an under-display Face ID sensor and camera on the outer screen. However, he suggests the technology could arrive with either the second or third generation, so its inclusion in the next model remains uncertain.


						

							




iPhone Duo cameras: What cameras does it have?

				
					

				
			
There are two cameras on the rear.

Apple




The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:


CameraResolutionEquivalent focal lengthAperture

Fusion Main48MP26mmf/1.6
2x crop from Main12MP52mmf/1.6
Fusion Ultra Wide48MP13mmf/2.2
Outer front camera12MP—f/2.2
Inner FaceTime cameraApple does not specify resolution—f/1.8

 



The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.


The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo
Duo Preview
The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.
Smart Take and Kid Cue
Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.
Two-screen shooting
The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.
Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.


						

							


Rear cameras
The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.
The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.
That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.
Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.
Front cameras
On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.
Inside is an under-display FaceTime camera with an f/1.8 aperture. Apple does not specify its megapixel resolution. It supports Center Stage for video calls and records at up to 1080p/60fps. Its major advantage is visual rather than photographic: the camera effectively disappears beneath the display when it isn’t being used.
iPhone Duo video features
The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.
Apple’s specifications also do not list ProRes or Apple Log recording for the Duo. Those remain more Pro-oriented capabilities rather than part of Apple’s foldable camera proposition.
The Duo does support Spatial Audio recording, Audio Mix, Dolby Vision HDR and Apple’s computational photography features including Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5, Photographic Styles 3, smart focus tracking and Apple Intelligence-powered editing.
Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.


						

							


iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

				
					

				
			
Watch video on the screen.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.
The A20 Pro includes:
6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
Dual 16-core Neural Engine
Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays
Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.
Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.


						

							


iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?
Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.
Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models. 
Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.
Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.


						

							


iPhone Duo connectivity

				
					

				
			
An expensive desk calendar. 

Apple




Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.
It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.
The N1 wireless networking chip provides:
Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
Bluetooth 6
Thread networking
The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.
The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.
It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.
iPhone Handoff – a feature introduced with iOS 27 – makes it easier to use an iPhone Duo alongside another iPhone without needing separate phone numbers. Both devices share your number, with calls, voicemail, messages and Find My location following whichever iPhone you unlock. Only one phone is active at a time. You could use the Duo’s folding display for work, then switch to an iPhone Pro when you want its telephoto camera. Both phones need iOS 27, eSIM support and the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled. Your carrier must specifically support iPhone Handoff, and your plan may require an additional monthly fee for access. T-Mobile already offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month; Verizon and EE (in the U.K.) plan support. Fees may apply.
Satellite capabilities include:
Emergency SOS via satellite
Roadside Assistance via satellite
Find My via satellite
Messages via satellite


						

							


Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?
Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.
Apple rates battery life at:
Up to 24 hours of typical use
Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
Up to 31 hours using the inner display
Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display
Early reviewers reported different battery experiences. CNET found the Duo comfortably lasted through a busy day, while The Verge questioned whether it could manage a full day of heavy use. These observations reflect different usage patterns and testing methods, so they should not be treated as directly comparable results or replacements for Apple’s playback ratings above.
Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.
Apple says the iPhone Duo can reach 50 percent charge in around 20 minutes using a USB-C charging cable and a 60W-capable power adapter or higher.
MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging are supported at up to 25W. Apple’s claimed 50 percent charge in around 30 minutes requires a MagSafe charger paired with a 35W-or-higher power adapter.
In both the U.S. and U.K., the box includes the iPhone Duo and a 1-meter USB-C charging cable, but no power adapter. The MagSafe charger is also sold separately, so factor these accessories into your budget if you don’t already own suitable equipment.


						

							




iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.
Prices are:


StoragePrice

256GB$1,999/£1,999
512GB$2,199/£2,199
1TB$2,599/£2,599
2TB$3,199/£3,199

 



The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.


iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.
That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.
Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.


						

							


iPhone Duo software: Multitasking and Apple Pencil support
The iPhone Duo’s larger inner display enables Split View, letting you use two apps side by side. For example, you could keep Safari open while taking notes, or check your calendar alongside a conversation in Messages. Supported apps can also open two windows of their own: Safari can display two webpages side by side for comparison shopping. You can save pairs of apps to return to later.
Early reviews suggest that third-party apps do not yet make good use of the larger display. Tom’s Guide and Wired encountered apps with black bars around them, while Tom’s Guide also reported poorly fitting game layouts. 
App support is improving, however. Apple has highlighted that Netflix, Fantastical, MLB and Asphalt Legends will be among the apps optimized for launch, and says compatible apps carry a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their App Store product pages. Other updates are still coming: Microsoft Word and Outlook’s Duo-specific layouts are due in the coming weeks, while Zenless Zone Zero’s update is scheduled for November. 
StandBy also works differently on the Duo. Set the phone down and it can display a clock, photos or widgets on either screen without being connected to a charger. New Calendar and Weather faces join the existing options.
Apple Pencil support is coming later in 2026. Apple has announced compatibility with the Apple Pencil (USB-C), allowing users to write, sketch and mark up documents on either display.


						

							


What do the first iPhone Duo reviews say? 
The first independent reviews praise the Duo’s hinge, display and overall hardware design, while highlighting uneven app optimization and differing battery experiences. Reviewers generally enjoyed the folding experience, but their findings reinforce the importance of checking whether it suits your everyday needs.


						

							


Should you buy the iPhone Duo?
The iPhone Duo is the iPhone to buy if you genuinely want a phone and small tablet in one device. Its 7.6-inch display, multitasking features, A20 Pro performance and clever fold-specific camera modes offer capabilities no other iPhone has. 
But at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 
For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is likely to be the better-value flagship. Buy the Duo because you want the folding experience, not because it is simply the “best” iPhone.

title: MacBook Neo Helps Apple Outpace Rivals as Market Declines
content:
Apple increased its share of worldwide PC shipments in the third quarter of 2026, with Counterpoint Research crediting the MacBook Neo for some of the company's resilience during a market downturn.


The firm's preliminary estimates put Mac shipments at 5.6 million units, an 11% decrease from the same quarter last year. Worldwide PC shipments fell 21% to 57 million units, allowing Apple's market share to increase from 8.7% to 9.8%. Counterpoint identified the ‌MacBook Neo‌ as a key contributor to Apple's performance.

The report explains how rising production costs are making replacement computers harder to afford. Higher memory and component prices have fed through to PC prices, prompting consumers to postpone purchases. Business fleet replacements and Windows migration sustained some demand, although neither was enough to prevent the overall contraction.

Apple remained the fourth-largest PC vendor by shipments. Lenovo led with a 26.3% share, followed by HP at 18.1% and Dell at 13.3%. Shipments at those companies declined 23%, 31%, and 25%, respectively.

ASUS, in fifth-place, was the only vendor among the top five to record a smaller annual decline than Apple. Its shipments fell 7%, giving it a 9.2% market share.

title: Happy 25th Anniversary, iPod
content:
Apple today marks 25 years since the introduction of the original iPod, one of the company's most significant products and a major contributor to its expansion beyond the Mac.


Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPod on October 23, 2001, at a small press event in the Town Hall auditorium at Apple's Infinite Loop headquarters. Advertised as offering "1,000 songs in your pocket," the device combined a 5GB hard drive with a monochrome LCD display, a mechanical scroll wheel, and up to 10 hours of battery life.

The original model cost $399 and required a Mac with iTunes. Its FireWire connection transferred music and charged the battery, while automatic synchronization copied songs and playlists from the user's iTunes library. Apple said that an entire CD could be transferred in under 10 seconds and a collection of 1,000 songs in less than 10 minutes. The hard drive could also store documents and other files.




MacRumors rumor roundup published two days before the event included the name "iPod."

original coverage is still available, along with reader comments questioning the device's price, Mac-only compatibility, and significance. One reader described it as "far from revolutionary," while another wrote, "all this hype for something so ridiculous!"


The iPod went on sale on November 10, 2001, with readers reporting that they lined up to purchase it. Early forum discussions included complaints about fingerprints on the polished rear enclosure, charging temperatures, and sound quality, alongside a host of positive impressions from owners.

Hardware revisions followed in quick succession. The second-generation iPod adopted a touch-sensitive scroll wheel, while the third-generation model introduced the 30-pin Dock Connector in 2003. The full-size iPod gained a color display in 2004 and video playback in 2005.

The iPod mini was announced in January 2004, representing the first extension of the product line. It featured a smaller anodized aluminum enclosure in silver, gold, pink, blue, or green, and introduced the Click Wheel, which integrated playback buttons into the touch-sensitive scrolling surface. Apple adopted the same control for the fourth-generation full-size iPod later that year.

In 2005, Apple introduced both the iPod shuffle and iPod nano. The shuffle omitted a display and offered a smaller, simpler music player, while the nano replaced the mini with a thin design based on flash storage. Later iPod nano models added video playback, a video camera, and a touchscreen. The square sixth-generation model, introduced in 2010, could be worn on the wrist using third-party watch straps.

sold 100 million iPods, less than six years after the first model reached customers. By its 10th anniversary in 2011, sales had exceeded 304 million units.

iPod touch arrived in September 2007, several months after the first iPhone went on sale. It featured a 3.5-inch Multi-Touch display, Wi-Fi, and Safari, without requiring a cellular plan. 

iPod classic in September 2014, five years after its final hardware revision. The iPod nano and iPod shuffle followed in July 2017, leaving the iPod touch as the sole model.


The seventh-generation iPod touch received an A10 Fusion chip and up to 256GB of storage in May 2019. It remained on sale without further hardware updates until May 10, 2022, when Apple announced its discontinuation and said it would be available while supplies lasted.

announcement, Apple attributed the end of the lineup to the integration of music playback across its other products. Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said that "the spirit of iPod lives on" through devices including the iPhone, Apple Watch, HomePod mini, Mac, iPad, and Apple TV.

title: iPhone Duo Launch Begins as First Orders Reach Customers
content:
It's already Friday, October 23 in Australia and New Zealand, which means customers who pre-ordered an iPhone Duo are beginning to receive their devices.


We are seeing first impressions and early photos from actual customers on the MacRumors forums, Instagram, Reddit, and other social networks. If your ‌iPhone Duo‌ has been delivered, let us know what you think of it in the comments below. MacRumors reader Boardiesboi is always one of the first to get a new iPhone and share images. 

Priced starting at $1,999, the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is Apple's first foldable device, featuring a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display.


Apple says retail stores in select countries will have a limited number of iPhone Duos for walk-in purchases on launch day, and it expects stock to sell out fast due to "extraordinary" demand. There is no Apple Store in New Zealand, so store stock in Australia will give us an idea of what in-store availability might look like worldwide.


Apple Stores in the United States, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Italy (select stores), Mexico, Macao (launch day only), Germany, the Netherlands, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the UK will have some iPhone Duos for walk-in customers.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ will not be available for walk-in purchase in France, China, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates, so customers in those locations will need a reservation for ‌Apple Store‌ pickup.

Apple's website advises customers to check back on Saturday, October 24 for pickup reservations. Shipping estimates for online orders slipped to January 25 shortly after pre-orders started and have stayed there since. Purchasing on launch day or getting lucky with a pickup reservation at a later date is the best chance of getting an ‌iPhone Duo‌ this year.

It's possible some carriers and big-box stores could also have stock available on launch day.

title: 1Password for Agents Keeps Your Passwords Hidden From AI
content:
Popular password management app 1Password today announced 1Password for Agents, a platform that gives AI agents safe access to user credentials for completing tasks.



The platform lets AI agents access logins, passwords, and other data without seeing or storing the information. Agents can send a request to sign in to a website or account, and users can approve or deny the request. 1Password says the agent uses a unique digital key to verify its identity, and then the login information is filled directly into the sign-in form.

Personal AI agents like Meta Muse, ChatGPT Dots, and Claude Duet often need access to accounts and sensitive user information, and 1Password for Agents offers that access without exposing passwords.

1Password for Agents is rolling out "over the coming days" for Grok Bot and Muse. Claude Duet, ChatGPT Work and Dots, and Town's Townie integrations are "coming soon."

title: iPhone Duo 24 Hours Later: Your Questions Answered
content:
MacRumors videographer Dan Barbera got his iPhone Duo a day early, so he spent today answering some of the questions people are asking about the new device.



On app optimization, some apps scale to fill the Duo's screen, and others have been updated for the actual Duo form factor with unique features for the different positions. Netflix has a special mode for a half-fold, for example.

There are apps that haven't been updated at all, and those have thick black bars on the sides. The apps are usable, but it's not a good experience. We'll see a ton of app updates coming out starting tomorrow, so hopefully unoptimized apps become less of a problem. Multitasking with two apps side by side is useful, and it's nice to be able to do things like watch a video while scrolling a website.

iPhone 17 camera. It's not as good as the iPhone 18 Pro camera with a variable aperture, but it's not terrible. There is no telephoto lens, and camera quality is one of the big ‌iPhone Duo‌ compromises. The under-display Face ID camera is okay for casual FaceTime videos, but the quality is comparatively poor for anything else.

Touch ID is not as quick as ‌Face ID‌, especially because Apple built a deliberate pause into it. You need to touch and hold to unlock. The Apple Watch can be used to unlock the ‌iPhone Duo‌, and that's an experience that's closer to ‌Face ID‌.

iPad with a nano-texture display. It does pick up fingerprints, but it doesn't feel like it's going to break or scratch easily.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ is heavier than other iPhones, and it can feel bulky. Depending on hand size, you may be able to use it one-handed, though it's harder to use left-handed because the the ‌Touch ID‌ button and on-screen navigation bars are on the right.

At a $1,999 starting price, the Duo is expensive, and it has compromises that will deter some people. Once major apps get updated, the experience will change, and we'll have a better idea of whether it's worth getting.

title: Trying to snag an iPhone Duo? These stock-checking sites might help
content:
Macworld





Ah, the stock-tracking site. When that must-have gadget is hard to get, they can help you find some limited retail or online restock before it disappears.
We see them all the time when there’s a new game console launch, or some hard-to-find sneakers, or during that brief Stanley Cup craze. But it has been a while since an iPhone launch has needed one. Sometimes a specific iPhone color is out of stock, but the situation is usually rectified quickly. Between Apple’s site offering a reasonable delivery estimate, carrier stores, and a fast retail refresh, the iPhone you want is usually not too hard to find. 
Usually. But the iPhone Duo is different. Notoriously difficult to manufacture and thus in limited supply, preorders at launch are now stretching into late January of 2027. That’s a three-month wait if you order now. You might do better buying an iPhone Duo from your carrier. Or trying to grab one of the modest retail resupplies that will trickle out over the coming weeks. That’s where stock-checking sites come in.
iPhoneStockChecker shows you nearby stock in various colors and storage sizes. It includes the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well, which can still be a little hard to get in particular storage/color combinations.
OrionChime has two sub-sites. One checks restaurant availability in Japan (really), and the other checks on stock for Apple products like iPhones, Mac Studio, or Mac mini.
Apple Inventory Check also checks inventory for various Apple products, including Macs and Apple Watch, and of course iPhones (including Duo). It’s limited to Apple Stores, but it’s faster than using the interface on Apple’s site to check availability of various configurations.
TrackaLacker is a general stock-tracking site for online retailers. You can watch iPhone Duo there, but only for the online stores of places like Best Buy or Walmart, not the Apple Store online or in-store stock.
Most of these will also let you set a browser notification to alert you when a particular product or configuration is spotted, or even an email, but continually checking and notifying you is often a paid feature, or at least requires signing up for a free account with the site. (AI agents or tools like Apple’s new Notify Me feature in Safari might let you keep tabs on things, too.)

The early reviews of the iPhone Duo posted on Wednesday, and one common complaint is how some third-party apps look on the device. The iPhone Duo has new dimensions, and that often results in a suboptimal user experience. One reviewer went so far as to call them “horrible.”
In these situations, apps are not yet optimized for the iPhone Duo. Apps that are made for iPhone Duo can provide quite rewarding experiences, as Apple points out in an article it released to the media on Thursday. “From watching popular shows and content on the expansive inner display to multitasking across windows or playing console-quality games, developers around the world are reimagining what their apps can do,” said Apple VP Susan Prescott in the press release.

				
					

				
			
Netflix on the iPhone Duo.

Apple




Video apps are taking advantage of the bigger folding display by providing modes that work when the Duo is propped open in an L shape; the top display shows the video while the bottom can display video controls and other items, as shown on the Netflix app. The Paramount+ app does a similar thing, but the bottom display can show info on the show being watched.
Sports fans can have a great time watching the game in apps made for iPhone Duo. The screen can be split so that live game coverage is streamed on one half, while the other provides a vast array of statistics, scores, and other data, as with the MLB app, which will be available on day one, in time for the World Series.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Productivity apps such as Bear, Fantastical, Notewise, Salesforce, Slack, Things, and Zoom take advantage of the larger inner display, and Microsoft Word and Outlook take advantage of the Duo’s Split View. Creative apps such as Detail, Instagram Edits, and VLLO provide an enhanced UI for video editing. Apple says apps that have been optimized will have a clear “Made for iPhone Duo” badge in the App Store.
Of course, games provide a better experience on the Duo’s big screen. Game such as Asphalt Legends, Retrocade, Sneaky Sasquatch, Ungodly, Zenless Zone Zero have been optimized for the new phone. “The large inner display and the sustained performance of A20 Pro let us put more of the track and every detail of our cars in front of users, so races look and feel incredible wherever they play,” said Raúl Orrego del Río, of Gameloft, creator of Asphalt Legends.
While Apple’s press release lists several more apps optimized for iPhone Duo, there are still many more that are not. It’s not a new situation; when Apple introduced the iPad, iPhone 5, and iPhone X, several developers had their apps ready for the device launch, but a vast majority were not. Developers need some time to catch up, so if your favorite app looks odd on your iPhone Duo, be sure to check the App Store for updates. There could be one waiting for your Duo.
Macworld will be posting an in-depth review of the iPhone Duo soon. In the meantime, check out our guide to everything you need to know about the iPhone Duo.

title: Critical PHP vulnerabilities threaten your NAS, not every vendor has a fix
content:
Attackers are actively exploiting critical PHP flaws to target internet-exposed NAS devices. If your files and backups are stored there, they're probably at risk.

TerraMaster Network Attached Storage
PHP2Shell refers to two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a scripting language used by web servers and some NAS services. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, could allow attackers to execute code on affected servers without logging in.
The PHP development team released security updates on October 21 for versions 8.2 through 8.5. The urgency isn't hypothetical, as Amazon detected an attempted exploit on October 17, four days before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed.
For NAS owners, the threat affects both software maintained by the manufacturer and applications running independently in Docker containers. In either case, the risk of a remote attack depends on whether attackers can reach the vulnerable PHP service.

Apps built with the iOS 27 SDK fill most of the inner display on the iPhone Duo, but they still avoid the status bar on the right edge.

Apps built with the iOS 26 SDK or earlier run on the iPhone Duo, but the app will appear in the center of the inner display with lots of empty space on each side.


Many more apps are being optimized for the iPhone Duo each and every day, so keep a close eye on the App Store's updates menu.

title: The iPhone Duo 2 might fix one of its biggest flaws
content:
Macworld





The iPhone Duo hits stores tomorrow, and the anticipation couldn’t be higher. Pre-orders are backordered until January, although Apple has confirmed that limited quantities will be available for walk-in customers on launch day. Apple Stores are already preparing for big crowds, and basically everyone who’s tried one is ready to declare it the best foldable of the year. 
But those early reviews aren’t all glowing. There’s an issue with app compatibility, which should be solved relatively quickly. Some people have lamented the lack of a telephoto lens. And others took issue with the battery life.
However, the biggest issue by far is the lack of Face ID. Due to the complexity of the double-screen design and the TrueDepth camera system, Apple opted to use Touch ID as the only unlocking/authentication biometric on the Duo. That means more fumbling and less convenience when wearing gloves or holding a drink. But according to a report from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, Apple is looking to solve this as soon as possible.
On his new Power On podcast, Gurman spills some details he’s heard about the next generations of iPhone Duo:
But here’s what I’ve heard. There are a few different features that Apple is already looking at for the iPhone Duo 2 and the iPhone Duo 3. One thing that Apple has been actively working on, is under display Face ID.
And you saw, they took a bigger step towards that with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this year, where they made the Dynamic Island much smaller. They moved more of the components under the display. I’m told there are iPhone Duo 2 prototypes at Apple already that have an under display Face ID sensor and camera on the outside screen.
None of that is a surprise, of course. Apple generally holds back features that either aren’t cost-effective or can’t be implemented in the way Apple wants. The Face ID issue is probably a little of both, so it could take a little longer to reach a production device. Gurman predicts that the issue will be solved “by the first update or the second update. So in the next two to three years or so.
With iPhone Duo stock limited and online delivery estimates already stretching into 2027, you could be waiting until next year to get your hands on one anyway. At that point, it might make more sense to just wait for the 2nd-generation model.

The worst time to buy an iPhone
This is generally in the weeks leading up to Apple’s September launch event, or in the early spring, when new models are expected to be announced. Buying just before a refresh means you could miss out on new features or pay full price for a model that’s about to be superseded.
The best time to buy an iPhone 
This depends on where you live:
In the U.K., where most iPhones are sold unlocked and off contract, the biggest savings are typically available during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day (usually in July and October, and occasionally in March) and Black Friday in late November. However, worthwhile iPhone discounts can be found throughout the year if you know where to look.
In the U.S., where people tend to buy iPhones through a carrier, the best time to upgrade is often during Black Friday when networks enhance their offers with larger trade-in values, bill credits, gift cards, or discounted service plans. 


						

							







Should you buy a new iPhone now or wait? 

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




September and the months that follow are a much better time to buy an iPhone than earlier in the summer. July and August are usually poor months to buy a Pro iPhone because Apple’s September launch is so close. The iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo have now been unveiled, removing that uncertainty.
If you need a phone now, there’s little reason to wait for another annual refresh, and the iPhone 17, 17e and Air are also relatively safe purchases because their successors aren’t expected until spring 2027. See: iPhone 18 and 18e rumors and iPhone Air 2 rumors. 
The iPhone 17 remains the strongest value, with a 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage for $899/£899 (although it was previously $799/£799). The 18 Pro and Pro Max make more sense if you want the best cameras, performance or battery life, while the Duo is for buyers specifically interested in Apple’s new folding design.
There is, however, one important reason to wait: 2027 could bring a much bigger iPhone redesign. Apple is rumored to be preparing a 20th-anniversary iPhone with a near-all-screen curved design, under-display Face ID, possible solid-state buttons, a thinner and more efficient OLED display, larger battery and major camera improvements. That could make 2027 a more significant upgrade year than 2026.
So if your current iPhone is still serving you well, waiting could be worthwhile. Otherwise, buy now if you need a phone, or wait until Black Friday if price is your main concern.

When does Apple release new iPhones?
Apple has a well-established pattern of releasing new iPhones every year, typically in September. This annual cycle has been remarkably consistent for over a decade, with only rare exceptions. 
While September remains the anchor for high-end models, Apple has begun to stagger its iPhone launches. Starting with the iPhone 16e in early 2025 and continuing with the iPhone 17e in spring 2026, Apple now releases more affordable models at separate events earlier in the year – often in March. 
Apple announced the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo in September 2026, but their availability differed: the Pro models went on sale September 18, while the Duo goes on sale October 23. The standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 are expected to follow in spring 2027.
September launches are usually accompanied by a dedicated Apple keynote, while spring releases are more likely to be announced via a press release although Apple has held spring events. Following the announcement, Apple typically opens pre-orders within a few days, with devices going on sale one to two weeks later. Initial availability can be limited, particularly for the most popular models and storage configurations.
How to check iPhone stock near you
If the iPhone you want has a long delivery estimate, independent stock-checking services can help you find availability elsewhere. Apple Inventory Check lets you search Apple Store stock by country, location, model, color and storage capacity. It covers Apple’s current iPhone range, including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and older models.
Checking nearby stores or choosing a different color or capacity could help you get your phone sooner. Confirm availability through Apple before traveling. For more options, see our guide to iPhone stock-checking services.


						

							


Should you wait for the iPhone 18?
For most people, there isn’t a strong reason to wait for the iPhone 18. Apple isn’t expected to launch the standard model until spring 2027, so buying an iPhone 17 before the end of 2026 would still give you several months with Apple’s current mainstream model before its replacement arrives.
The iPhone 18 is expected to bring a 2nm A20 chip, potentially 9GB or 12GB of RAM, Apple’s C2 modem and possibly a new 24MP front camera. Extra RAM could prove particularly useful for future Apple Intelligence and Siri features. However, the rear camera system is still expected to consist of two 48MP cameras, while the display may remain broadly similar to the iPhone 17’s 6.3-inch ProMotion panel.
There is also some uncertainty over exactly what the iPhone 18 lineup will look like. A September 2026 rumour suggested Apple could effectively merge the standard iPhone and iPhone Air into a single model, rather than continuing them as two separate devices. If that happens, the iPhone 18 could adopt some of the Air’s thinner, lighter design while retaining the broader appeal of the standard iPhone. For now, though, that remains speculative.
Price is another consideration. With the arrival of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, Apple increased iPhone prices across the range, so the iPhone 17 now costs $899, $100 more than at launch. When the iPhone 18 arrives, it is likely to inherit that $899 price point, while the iPhone 17 could drop back to around $799 at which you may regret buying it at the higher price.
Wait if you want the newer A20 chip, potentially more RAM, an improved front camera, or are intrigued by the possibility of a thinner redesigned standard model. 
Don’t wait if you simply want ProMotion, dual 48MP cameras, excellent battery life and 256GB of storage as standard – the iPhone 17 already delivers all of that.

 FAQ 


1.
When is the best carrier upgrade timing? 
Apple typically announces new iPhone models in September. Carriers often roll out their most aggressive trade-in offers and promotional deals around this time to entice customers to upgrade.
New releases: Waiting for the September (or spring) launch window is generally a good strategy if you want the latest model at a potentially better subsidized price.
Check your contract cycle: Many carrier contracts today last 24 to 36 months. If you’re nearing the end of your contract, you’re in a strong position to negotiate or take advantage of upgrade offers. However, upgrading mid-contract may involve paying off the remaining balance, so it’s worth checking your specific terms.
Consider Apple’s upgrade plans: Apple has replaced its old iPhone Upgrade Program with newer financing and leasing options. In the U.S., Apple Upgrade lets you lease an iPhone through Klarna and upgrade, buy or return it at the end of the term. In the U.K., Apple’s Flexible Finance Account offers eligible iPhones on monthly payment plans with the option to upgrade after a set number of payments. Terms and monthly costs vary by model.





2.
When does Apple update the iPhone?
Apple follows a well-established annual rhythm for its iPhone updates, with the primary event taking place in September each year. 
Apple typically unveils its new iPhone lineup at a dedicated Apple Event in September. Pre-orders usually open on the Friday following the announcement, with devices shipping and arriving in stores a week later. 
Apple also occasionally introduces new iPhones outside the September window and in the past it has held a Spring Apple Event at which more affordable iPhones have launched. The iPhone 17e, for example, arrived in March 2026, and the iPhone 16e launched in February 2025. 
Compatible iPhone models also get a yearly operating system software update with new features that can make your old iPhone feel new again. The major iOS updates follow the September schedule.
Read our guide to the next Apple event to find out if an Apple event is imminent.





3.
When do iPhone prices drop and by how much?
Based on past experience, Apple is very unlikely to reduce the price of a new iPhone during its first year on sale.
However, when Apple introduces a new generation of iPhones, it usually cuts the price of the previous year’s models. That means September has traditionally been the point when older iPhones become cheaper.
Apple also tends to keep launch prices broadly similar from one generation to the next, at least in the U.S., although exchange rates and other regional factors can affect pricing elsewhere.
In 2024, for example, Apple reduced the price of the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus by $100/£100 when the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus arrived. The iPhone 16 also fell in price following the launch of the iPhone 17 in 2025. However, because the iPhone 17 doubled the base storage to 256GB, the older iPhone 16 looked less attractive even at $100/£100 less.
In 2026, the pattern changed. Apple actually raised iPhone prices, blaming higher memory costs. Even the year-old iPhone 17 and two-year-old iPhone 16 increased by $100, showing that older iPhones don’t always become cheaper when a new generation arrives.





4.
Is it better to buy from Apple or a carrier?
In the U.S., buying from Apple is usually the better option if you value flexibility. If you pay in full or use Apple’s own financing, the iPhone is unlocked, so you can switch carriers or use another eSIM when traveling. Apple also accepts trade-ins and, importantly, many AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon promotions are available when buying through Apple.
However, an iPhone bought from Apple but financed through an AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon device-payment plan is locked to that carrier until it has been paid off. An iPhone bought outright from Apple isn’t.
The main reason to buy directly from AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon is to take advantage of a particularly good promotion. U.S. carriers frequently advertise large trade-in credits or “free” iPhones, especially when you add a line or switch networks. The catch is that the discount is usually provided as monthly bill credits over 24 or 36 months, so if you leave early you can lose the remaining credits.
In the U.K., Apple sells iPhones unlocked and SIM-free, allowing you to shop separately for a SIM-only plan from EE, Vodafone, O2, Three or an MVNO. This makes it easier to switch networks and can work out cheaper over the life of the phone than bundling the handset and airtime into a single contract.
Apple isn’t necessarily the cheapest place to buy, however. Amazon U.K. and other retailers frequently discount SIM-free iPhones, and there can be substantial savings during sales events such as Black Friday.
Networks can also offer compelling promotions, including enhanced trade-in values, discounted airtime, generous data allowances or lower monthly payments. But make sure you compare the total cost of the contract, rather than focusing on the headline monthly price.





5.
When are the best iPhone deals?
The earliest you could expect to get a discount on the newest iPhones is around Black Friday at the end of November, so you might be planning to hold out until then. However, the deals we tend to see, if any, are usually for older handsets. See our round-up of Best Black Friday iPhone deals for more.
Nor should you expect to get a discount in an Apple Black Friday sale. Apple’s Black Friday sale usually only takes the form of vouchers with select product purchases, rather than a discount, and it is unlikely that the newest iPhone would qualify as in previous year’s new iPhones haven’t been included. 
Note that while shopping events like Black Friday get all the attention, that’s not the only time you can get discounts on Apple products: we see discounts all the time. Another event where we see good iPhone deals is Prime Day, which happens in June or July and October every year. So take a look at the iPhone deals for Amazon Prime Day sale to see what you might be able to save.
In our experience, we don’t tend to see discounts on the newest handset until the spring – and these are always from third-party resellers, never from Apple. In fact, we don’t tend to see the iPhone discounted in the U.S. very often, most of the discounts we see are in the U.K. where unlocked iPhones are often sold off-contract at a good discount.





6.
Is it worth buying a refurbished iPhone? 
Yes, buying a refurbished iPhone is absolutely worth it for most people, especially if you want to save money without sacrificing quality. 
Buying refurbished is a great way to “pick up a bargain” while still getting a premium device. You can typically save 15% to 30% compared to buying new, and sometimes much more on older models. 
A common misconception is that refurbished is the same as buying a used phone from a stranger, though. It’s not. A used phone is sold “as-is,” with no guarantee it will work properly. A refurbished phone has been professionally inspected, tested, and repaired if needed, and it comes with a warranty. 
If you want the highest quality, Apple’s own refurbished store is the gold standard.





Conclusion: When is the best time to buy a new iPhone?
The worst time to buy is usually between July or August, mainly because with new iPhones on the horizon the price of the older handsets are likely to drop very soon.
If you want the newest iPhones then the best deals don’t tend to come before the spring and summer months. If you are happy to buy an older iPhone then you will probably see decent deals around Prime Day and Black Friday – but deals happen all year round. 
We hope this article has proved helpful in reaching an informed buying decision. Remember that good prices can be found all year round, if a retailer is feeling generous and you know where to look: read our guide to the best iPhone deals for more on that.

title: 5 features I want in the new MacBook Pro (other than a touchscreen)
content:
Macworld





The MacBook Pro, as we know it, isn’t long for Apple’s Mac lineup. It’s expected to undergo a drastic change during next week’s “Pro and Tell” event. At long last, Apple is expected to unveil its long-rumored MacBook Pro that finally brings touchscreen support to the Mac.
A touchscreen alone, however, isn’t enough to sell me on an upgrade. I already have an iPhone and an iPad. For one, Apple needs to convince me that I even want a touchscreen on my MacBook Pro, but more than that, the touchscreen makeover is a perfect opportunity for Apple to upgrade its laptop in other ways. Here’s what I’ll be looking for when Apple unveils the first touchscreen MacBook Pro next week.
A new macOS
To be completely honest, I’m not really excited about a touchscreen on a MacBook Pro. I’m unable to imagine how the way I use my Mac can be enhanced by my fingers on the display. So this is the number one thing I’ll be looking for, way above anything else: I want to see how Apple plans to implement touch input in macOS.
It has to be more than, say, being able to tap and drag Safari tabs with accompanying visual effects, as was leaked recently. I need to see more than larger elements to accompany touch. I need to see features that will make me want to reach out and poke my display and think the inevitable fingerprints are worth it. For example, in a conversation here in the Macworld office, Jason Cross mused that iPhone Mirroring could have some advantages if you’re able to physically interact with the projection as you would the device itself. That’s the kind of interesting and novel new feature I’d like to see.
Touchscreen laptops aren’t a new idea, which means Apple has had plenty of time to experiment and develop a touch UI. But lots of people, including many who should be the target audience for a MacBook Pro, have used macOS for years and will need to see something truly innovative to consider buying one. I hope I see that next week, though I won’t be surprised if we have to wait until WWDC next June to see some real change.
Lighter design
The other day at the Macworld office, I had my 16-inch MacBook Pro in my backpack. I put my backpack on my desk, and it made a noticeable “thud.” Our office manager (an unabashed PC user) jokingly asked me why I carry a boat anchor around. I laughed, but he’s right: the MacBook Pro is very heavy.

				
					

				
			
Now that the MacBook Pro will have a vastly different feature set than the MacBook Air, there’s no need to make sure the MacBook Pro weighs more than the Air. 

Foundry




The 14-inch MacBook Pro weighs about 3.6 pounds (1.62 kg), while the 16-inch model is nearly 5 pounds (2.15 kg). By comparison, the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 is about a half-pound lighter. Rumors suggest that the new model will be significantly lighter than the current crop of MacBook Pros, so I’ll be looking closely at the tech specs to see just how much they weigh.
But a lighter MacBook Pro also needs to keep the same battery life, which is one of the best features of the MacBook Pro. A thinner and lighter battery is fine as long as Apple doesn’t sacrifice the existing battery life that has become the hallmark of Apple’s flagship laptops.
Face ID
Touch ID is great, but Face ID is better because it’s less disruptive and more immediate. A year ago, a report claimed that Face ID on a MacBook is “years away,” but plans tend to change very quickly in the tech world.
Back when Apple introduced the notch with the first M1 Pro/Max MacBook Pro, it seemed to be an obvious placeholder for an inevitable upgrade to Face ID. Five years later, that still hasn’t happened. This new MacBook Pro—which is expected to ditch the notch for an iPhone-like Dynamic Island—is a perfect opportunity to bring the convenience of facial recognition to the only camera you’re always staring at.

				
					

				
			
Is this the time that Apple can upgrade the FaceTime camera to a Face ID camera?

Foundry




5G connectivity
Apple once thought Macs and touchscreens should not go together, and it’s apparently changed its mind. Maybe it’s also changed its longstanding opinion that cellular connectivity doesn’t belong on a laptop. If hell is freezing over with the addition of a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro, why not add 5G connectivity too? Now that Apple has its own C-series modems that are super efficient and work with its own silicon without worry of battery life or connectivity issues, there’s no reason why Apple can’t offer the option to add 5G to the next MacBook Pro, just as it does with the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch.
A convertible 2-in-1
I’m not really sure what Apple has in store for the new design rumored for the touchscreen MacBook Pro, but my editor, Michael Simon, is wondering if Apple will do something truly different: Add a 360-degree hinge to turn it into a true macOS tablet. Apple has had a lot of time to work on its hinge tech with the iPhone Duo, so the touchscreen MacBook Pro could introduce something entirely new.
We’ve written for years about how the iPad hardware would be a perfect vehicle for a redesigned macOS for touch, and it would be interesting to see what a true tablet-ized version of macOS would look like. Could it support Apple Pencil? Will there be a virtual keyboard? As I said before, reaching out to touch my MacBook’s screen isn’t something I’m all that interested in, but a convertible design sure sounds tempting.

Apple’s 2026 iPhone lineup is broader than ever, ranging from the relatively affordable iPhone 17e to the high-end iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, plus the ultra-thin iPhone Air and the new folding iPhone Duo. That gives buyers more choice, but it also makes picking the right model more complicated than simply choosing the newest or most expensive iPhone.
For most people, the iPhone 17 is the best all-round choice, thanks to its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, strong battery life, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. The iPhone 17e is the better option if price matters most, while the iPhone 18 Pro is the model to choose for the best cameras and performance. The iPhone 18 Pro Max adds the longest battery life, the iPhone Air prioritises thinness and low weight, and the iPhone Duo offers Apple’s biggest and most flexible display.
Which iPhone is best for you will therefore depend on what you value most. Camera enthusiasts should look closely at the Pro models, heavy users may prefer the Pro Max for its battery life, while parents, older users and anyone trying to keep costs down may find the 17e a much better fit. There can also be excellent value in buying a discounted or refurbished older iPhone rather than paying full price for the latest hardware.
This guide focuses on the best iPhone to buy for different types of user and budget. If you want to dig deeper into the differences between every model, see our complete iPhone Buying Guide, where we compare the cameras, displays, performance, storage, battery life and other key specifications across Apple’s current lineup.

Why we recommend it
The iPhone 17 brings several features previously reserved for Pro models to Apple’s mainstream iPhone, including a 120Hz ProMotion display and Always-On support. It also offers the fast A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras, an improved Centre Stage selfie camera, strong battery life and 256GB of storage as standard. For most buyers, it strikes the best balance between price and features.
Buy iPhone 17 if
Buy the iPhone 17 if you want the best all-round iPhone without paying Pro prices. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, excellent cameras, strong battery life and 256GB starting storage make it particularly appealing to anyone upgrading from an iPhone 14 or older.
Don’t buy iPhone 17 if
Don’t buy it if you want optical zoom beyond 2x or Apple’s most advanced camera features—in that case, choose the iPhone 18 Pro. The iPhone Air is a better choice if thinness and low weight are your priorities, while existing iPhone 16 owners may find the upgrade relatively modest unless ProMotion and improved battery life are particularly important. 
What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 17e?
For the extra $200, the iPhone 17 gives you a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, Dynamic Island, a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera with macro photography, a brighter screen, stronger graphics performance, a better 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera and longer battery life. For most people who can afford the difference, it’s money well spent.
What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 16?
For $100 more, you get double the base storage at 256GB, a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, an upgraded 48MP Ultra Wide camera, an improved 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera, longer battery life, faster charging and the newer A19 processor. At full price, the iPhone 17 is the better buy.
Key specs
The iPhone 17 combines a 6.3-inch ProMotion display, Always-On support and the A19 chip with dual 48MP rear cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. It offers many of the features most people actually want from a Pro iPhone without the Pro price.
Starts at: $899 / £899 (was $799 / £799) for 256GB

Chip: A19

Cameras: 48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide, 18MP front camera
Battery: Up to 30 hours of video playback
Should you buy or wait?
Buy now. The iPhone 17 offers excellent value, while the iPhone 18 isn’t expected until spring 2027 and may bring higher prices rather than transformative upgrades. Waiting for Black Friday could make sense if you’re looking for a discount.
